concepts.title: Width
concepts.one_liner: The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width.
concepts.content: If you have a hidden layer with $N$ neurons, you can fit a scalar function with $\mathcal{O}(N)$ bumps. The number of neurons on a single hidden layer is called its width. If different layers have different numbers of neurons, then we may specify the width per layer. Here we will assume all layers have the same width and simply speak of the width of the network.
concepts.motivation_md: Width is a fundamental hyperparameter of neural networks that determines the capacity of a single layer to represent complex patterns or 'bumps' in a function.
concepts.recap_md:
- Width refers to the number of neurons in a specific hidden layer.
- Increasing width allows a network to fit more complicated functions with more features.

concepts.title: Depth
concepts.one_liner: The depth of a network is defined as its number of layers.
concepts.content: As we increase the width of a network, we can fit ever more complicated functions. Another way to increase the capacity of the net is to increase the depth of a network, which is its number of layers. Its effect on capacity is a bit different than increasing width.
concepts.motivation_md: Depth allows neural networks to learn hierarchical representations, where deeper layers build upon the features extracted by earlier layers.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth is the total number of layers in a neural network.
- Increasing depth is an effective way to increase the functional capacity of a model.

key_passage.text: What if we instead increase the depth of a network, that is, its number of layers? It turns out that this can also be an effective way to increase the capacity of the net, but its effect is a bit different than increasing width.

concepts.title: Depth separations
concepts.one_liner: Depth separations describe cases where deep nets require far fewer parameters than wide nets to represent certain functions.
concepts.content: Interestingly, it is sometimes the case that deep nets require far fewer parameters to fit data than wide nets. Evidence for this statement comes mostly from empiricism, where researchers have found that deeper nets just work better in practice on many popular problems. However, there is also the beginning of a mathematical theory of when and why this can happen. The basic idea of this theory is to establish that there are certain classes of function that can be represented with a polynomial number of neurons in a depth $d$ network but require an exponential number of neurons in a depth $d^\prime$ network, for certain $d^\prime < d$. Arguments along these lines are called depth separations.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept explains why deep architectures are often more efficient than shallow ones, providing a theoretical basis for the success of deep learning.
concepts.recap_md:
- Depth separations occur when a deep network can represent a function using polynomially many neurons while a shallower one requires exponentially many.
- This theory helps explain why deep networks often outperform wide, shallow networks in practice.

Arguments along these lines are called depth separations.

concepts.title: Hebbian learning

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Hebbian learning is a bottom-up approach where neurons wire up based on feedforward activity patterns rather than backpropagated errors.
concepts.content: One intriguing alternative to backpropagation is called Hebbian learning. Backpropagation is a top-down learning algorithm, where errors incurred at the output (top) of the net are propagated backward to inform earlier layers how to update their weights and biases to minimize the loss, which is a form of learning based on feedback. Hebbian learning, in contrast, is a bottom-up approach, where neurons wire up just based on the feedforward pattern of activity in the net. The canonical learning rule in Hebbian methods is Hebb's rule: "fire together, wire together." That is, we increase the weight of the connection between two neurons whenever the two neurons are active at the same time. Although this learning rule is not explicitly minimizing a loss function, it has been shown to lead to effective neural representations. For example, Hebb-like rules can learn infomax representations, which capture as much information as possible about the input signal, or lead to networks that act like memory banks. Hebbian learning is also of interest because it is considered to be more biologically plausible than backpropagation; Hebb's rule can be computed locally, whereas backpropagation requires global coordination.
concepts.motivation_md: Hebbian learning provides a biologically plausible alternative to backpropagation, focusing on local interactions rather than global error signals.
concepts.recap_md:
- Hebbian learning is a bottom-up, feedforward approach to updating neural weights.
- It relies on local rules where neurons that are active simultaneously strengthen their connections.
- It is considered more biologically plausible than backpropagation because it does not require global coordination.

This is because Hebb's rule can be computed locally---each neuron strengthens and weakens its weights based just on the activity of adjacent neurons---whereas backpropagation requires global coordination throughout the neural network.

concepts.title: Tensor

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: A tensor is a multidimensional array and the primary data structure used in deep learning.
concepts.content: The main data structure that we will encounter in deep learning is the tensor, which is just a multidimensional array. In general, everything in deep learning is represented as tensors—the input is one tensor, the activations are tensors, the weights are tensors, the outputs are tensors. If you have data that is not natively represented as a tensor, the first step is to convert it into a tensor format. Most often we use tensors of real numbers, where the elements are in $\mathbb{R}$. For example, a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ of images $\mathbf{x}$ and labels $\mathbf{y}$ can be viewed as two tensors: $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times C_0 \times H \times W }$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times K}$. The first dimension represents the number of elements in the dataset, while the remaining dimensions represent the dimensionality of the data (e.g., color channels, height, and width for images).
concepts.motivation_md: Tensors provide a unified mathematical framework for representing and processing high-dimensional data and model parameters efficiently.
concepts.recap_md:
- A tensor is a multidimensional array of values, typically real numbers.
- All components of a deep learning system (inputs, weights, activations) are represented as tensors.

concepts.title: Channels

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: Channels refer to the number of neurons in a layer, analogous to the color channels of an input image.
concepts.content: The activations in the network are also tensors. For the MLP networks we have seen so far, the activation tensors have shape $N \times C_{\ell}$, where $C_{\ell}$ is the number of neurons on layer $\ell$, sometimes also called channels in analogy to the color channels of the input image. In later architectures like convolutional networks, activation layers may have additional dimensions, such as shape $N \times C_{\ell} \times H_{\ell} \times W_{\ell}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of channels allows us to organize neural activations into distinct features or components, similar to how images are organized into color components.

- In MLPs, the channel dimension corresponds to the number of neurons $C_{\ell}$.

concepts.title: Learning with a Perceptron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron learns by adjusting weights and bias to minimize a classification loss that scores the number of misclassifications.
concepts.content:
A perceptron acts like a classifier that can learn from data. Given a dataset $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, we adjust the weights $\mathbf{w}$ and the bias $b$ to minimize a classification loss, $\mathcal{L}$, that scores the number of misclassifications:

$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{w}^*, b^* = \mathop{\mathrm{arg\,min}}_{\mathbf{w}, b} \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{x}^{(i)} + b, y^{(i)})
\end{aligned}$$

This optimization process corresponds to shifting and rotating the decision boundary until a line is found that separates data labeled as $y = 0$ from data labeled as $y = 1$.

(see figure: Different possible decision surfaces of a perceptron.)

While the original perceptron paper proposed a specific "perceptron learning algorithm," modern approaches typically use general-purpose optimizers. For differentiable objectives, gradient descent is used, while zeroth-order methods are preferred for nondifferentiable objectives like the threshold function used in the standard perceptron objective.
concepts.motivation_md: To use a perceptron as a practical classifier, we need a systematic way to find the weights and bias that best separate different classes of data. Learning provides a mathematical framework to optimize these parameters based on training examples.
concepts.recap_md: - Learning involves minimizing a classification loss $\mathcal{L}$ by adjusting weights $\mathbf{w}$ and bias $b$.

key_passage.text: The idea is that given data, we will adjust the weights and the bias, in order to minimize a classification loss, that scores the number of misclassifications.

concepts.title: Multilayer Perceptron
concepts.one_liner: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) is a network of neurons arranged in layers that can produce multiple outputs and solve non-linearly separable problems.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can solve linearly separable binary classification problems, but they are limited. We can achieve multiple outputs by adding edges that fan out after the perceptron.

(see figure: Multiple outputs fan out from a neuron.)

This network maps an input layer of data $\mathbf{x}$ to a layer of outputs $\mathbf{y}$. The neurons in between inputs and outputs are called hidden units. For example, $h = g(z)$ where $z$ is a hidden unit and $g(\cdot)$ is an activation function. More commonly, many hidden units are stacked in a multilayer perceptron (MLP).

(see figure: Mutilayer perceptron.)

The equation for this MLP is:
$$\begin{aligned}    \mathbf{z} &= \mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_1 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}\\
    \mathbf{h} &= g(\mathbf{z}) &\triangleleft \quad \text{activation function}\\
    \mathbf{y} &= \mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}_2 &\triangleleft \quad \text{linear layer}
\end{aligned}$$

MLPs can be constructed with any number of layers following the pattern of linear layer and activation function. The activation function $g$ can be any pointwise nonlinearity $\tilde{g}$ that maps $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. This sequence is the prototypical motif in almost all neural networks.
concepts.motivation_md: Single perceptrons are limited to linear classification and single outputs. MLPs overcome these limitations by stacking layers, allowing the network to learn complex, non-linear mappings and handle multiple output variables simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - An MLP consists of interleaved linear layers and pointwise activation functions.

key_passage.text: Because this network has multiple layers of neurons, and because each neuron in this net acts as a perceptron, we call it a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The equation for this MLP is: z = W₁x + b₁ (linear layer), h = g(z) (activation function), y = W₂h + b₂ (linear layer)

concepts.title: Activations and Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are the values neurons take on as data is processed, while parameters are the weights and biases learned by the network.
concepts.content:
In deep nets, it is useful to distinguish between activations and parameters. The activations are the values that the neurons take on, denoted as a sequence $[\mathbf{x}_0, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L]$, where $\mathbf{x}_0$ is the raw input data. These represent the neural representations of the data being processed.

[FIGURE:e4b298598d24ed71 | A multilayer network is a sequence of transformations $f_1, \ldots, f_L$ that produce a series of activations $\mathbf{x}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{x}_L$.]

Conversely, parameters are the weights and biases of the network, which are the variables being learned. Both activations and parameters are tensors. Each layer can be viewed as a function:
$$\begin{aligned}
    \mathbf{x}_{l+1} = f_{l+1}(\mathbf{x}_{l}, \theta_{l+1})
\end{aligned}$$
Each layer takes activations from the previous layer and parameters of the current layer to produce the next set of activations. This perspective allows for tricks like network prompting or visualization, where parameters are held fixed while activations are optimized.
concepts.motivation_md: Distinguishing between the data flowing through the network (activations) and the internal settings of the network (parameters) is essential for understanding how neural networks process information and how they are trained.
concepts.recap_md: - Activations are the neural representations of data as it passes through the network layers.

key_passage.text: The activations are the values that the neurons take on, $[\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}_1, \mathbf{h}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{z}_{L-1}, \mathbf{h}_{L-1}, \mathbf{y}]$; slightly abusing notation, we use this term for both preactivation function neurons and postactivation function neurons. Conversely, parameters are the weights and biases of the network. These are the variables being learned.

motivation.text: From this perspective, anything we can do with parameters, we can do with activations instead, and vice versa, and that is the basis for a lot of applications and tricks.

concepts.title: Fast Activations and Slow Parameters
concepts.one_liner: Activations are fast functions of individual datapoints, whereas parameters are slow functions learned from entire datasets.
concepts.content: Activations and parameters differ in their relationship to data. Activations are "fast" functions of a datapoint, resulting from a few layers of processing that specific input. Parameters are also functions of data, but they are "slow" functions of datasets, arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset. Both are statistics of the data: parameters act as a metasummary specifying a functional transformation, while activations are a summary of the individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: This distinction helps conceptualize the different timescales and scales of data involved in neural network operations: inference (fast, per-point) versus training (slow, per-dataset).
concepts.recap_md: - Activations change with every new input datapoint processed by the network.

key_passage.text: One way to think about it is that activations are *fast* functions of a data*point*: they are the result of a few layers of processing this datapoint. Parameters are *also* functions of the data (they are learned from data) but they are *slow* functions of data*sets*: the parameters are arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset.

motivation.text: So, both activations and parameters are statistics of the data, that is, information extracted about about the data that organizes or summarizes it. The parameters are a kind of metasummary since they specify a functional transformation that produces activations from data, and activations themselves are a summary of the data.

Parameters are *also* functions of the data (they are learned from data) but they are *slow* functions of data*sets*: the parameters are arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset.

Parameters are also functions of data, but they are "slow" functions of datasets, arrived at via an optimization procedure over a whole dataset. Both are statistics of the data: parameters act as a metasummary specifying a functional transformation, while activations are a summary of the individual datapoint.

concepts.title: Deep Nets
concepts.one_liner: Deep nets are neural networks that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times to perform complex nonlinear mappings.
concepts.content:
Deep nets are neural nets that stack the linear-nonlinear motif many times.

(see figure: Deep nets consist of linear layers interleaved with nonlinearities.)

Each layer is a function, making a deep net a composition of many functions:
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(\mathbf{x}) = f_{L}(f_{L-1}(\ldots f_2(f_1(\mathbf{x}))))
\end{aligned}$$
where $L$ is the number of layers. These functions are parameterized by weights $[\mathbf{W}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{W}_L]$ and biases $[\mathbf{b}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_L]$, collectively referred to as $\theta$. Deep nets are powerful because they can perform nonlinear mappings; with sufficiently many neurons, they can fit almost any desired function arbitrarily closely.
concepts.motivation_md: By composing many simple functions, deep nets can represent highly complex, non-linear relationships that shallower architectures cannot easily capture.
concepts.recap_md: - A deep net is a composition of $L$ functions, each representing a layer.

concepts.title: Rectified linear unit (relu)
concepts.one_liner: The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is a pointwise nonlinearity that yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, facilitating gradient-based learning.
concepts.content: The Rectified linear unit (relu) is a pointwise nonlinearity. It acts as a graded version of a threshold function. Its primary advantage is that it yields non-zero gradients over half its domain, making it highly amenable to gradient-based learning methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional threshold functions have zero gradients almost everywhere, which prevents gradient descent from working. ReLU provides a non-linear activation that still allows gradients to flow during training.

concepts.title: Universal approximation theorem
concepts.one_liner: The universal approximation theorem states that a neural network with a single hidden layer can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary precision.
concepts.content: The universal approximation theorem states that deep nets can, in principle, perform any continuous input-output mapping. This holds true even for a network with just a single hidden layer, provided the number of neurons in that layer is sufficiently large to fit complicated functions. Technically, this theorem applies to continuous functions on compact subsets of $\mathbb{R}^N$.
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the theoretical justification for using neural networks as general-purpose function approximators, ensuring that they are capable of representing the complex patterns found in real-world data.
concepts.recap_md: - A single hidden layer is sufficient to approximate any continuous function given enough neurons.

key_passage.text: The universal approximation theorem states that this is true even for a network with just a single hidden layer.

motivation.text: Not only can deep nets perform nonlinear classification, they can in principle perform any continuous input-output mapping.

concepts.title: Intuition for Universal Approximation
concepts.one_liner: Universal approximation works because a relu-MLP can represent a sum of indicator functions, which can approximate any curve.
concepts.content:
To understand universal approximation, consider approximating a function $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with a relu-MLP. Any function can be approximated by a sum of indicator functions (bumps):
$$\begin{aligned}
    f(x) \approx \sum_i w_i \mathbb{1}(\alpha_i < x < \beta_i)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: Any function from $\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be approximated arbitrarily well by a sum of elementary bumps.)

A relu-MLP can represent these bumps. While the weighted sum is handled by a linear layer, a single bump $\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta)$ can be approximated using four relu units:
$$\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{1}(\alpha < x < \beta) \approx \\
&\texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\alpha-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\alpha}{\gamma}\bigg) - \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-(\beta-\gamma)}{\gamma}\bigg) + \texttt{relu}\bigg(\frac{x-\beta}{\gamma}\bigg)
\end{aligned}$$

(see figure: A bump can be represented as a weighted sum of shifted and scaled relu functions.)

As $\gamma \rightarrow 0$, the approximation becomes exact. A `linear`-`relu`-`linear` network can implement this construction. By summing many such bumps, a single hidden layer network can approximate any curve to arbitrary precision, though the number of neurons required may be unbounded.
concepts.motivation_md: Visualizing how simple ReLU functions can be combined to create 'bumps' helps demystify how neural networks transform simple linear inputs into complex, arbitrary function approximations.
concepts.recap_md: - Any continuous function can be decomposed into a sum of small 'bumps' or indicator functions.

key_passage.text: First observe that any function can be approximated arbitrarily well by a sum of indicator functions, that is, bumps placed at different positions. As the width, β−α, of the bumps goes to zero, the error in the fit goes to zero.

motivation.text: Here we show how a neural net can represent a function as a sum of basis functions. This idea is also foundational in signal processing, where signals are often represented as a sum of sine waves, boxes, or trapezoids.

concepts.title: Neural Network
concepts.one_liner: Neural networks are functions loosely modeled on the brain's network of interconnected neurons.
concepts.content:
Neural networks are functions loosely modeled on the brain. In the brain, billions of neurons connect to one another, where each neuron can be thought of as a node in a graph and the edges are the connections between them.

(see figure: A neural network can be drawn as a directed graph.)

These edges are directed, meaning electrical signals propagate in one direction. Outgoing edges are called axons and incoming edges are called dendrites. A neuron fires, sending a pulse down its axon, when the incoming pulses from the dendrites exceed a certain threshold.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks provide a flexible, biologically-inspired architecture for approximating complex functions by composing simple processing units.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural networks are directed graphs of nodes representing neurons and edges representing connections.

concepts.title: Perceptron

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: A perceptron is a simple model of a single neuron that outputs a binary signal based on a weighted sum of its inputs.
concepts.motivation_md: The perceptron serves as the fundamental building block of neural networks, demonstrating how linear combinations and non-linear thresholds can perform basic computation.
concepts.recap_md: - A perceptron computes a weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, then applies a step-function activation.

key_passage.text: A perceptron is a neuron with n inputs {x_i}_{i=1}^n and one output y, that maps inputs to outputs according to the following equations: z = f(x) = sum_{i=1}^n w_i x_i + b = w^T x + b; g(z) = 1, if z > 0; 0, otherwise; y = g(f(x)).

motivation.text: In words, we take a weighted sum of the inputs and, if that sum exceeds a threshold (here 0), the neuron fires (outputs a 1).

concepts.title: The Perceptron as a Classifier

position.section_title: The Perceptron: A Simple Model of a Single Neuron

concepts.one_liner: Perceptrons can function as binary classifiers by splitting the input space into two regions.
concepts.content:
Perceptrons can learn to classify data by assigning class labels based on their output. For example, consider a perceptron with two inputs, $x_1$ and $x_2$, weights $w_1 = 2$, $w_2 = 1$, and bias $b=0$.

(see figure: Value of hidden unit ($z$) and output unit ($y$) in a perceptron, as a function of the input data.)

As shown in the figure, the output $y$ takes on values 0 or 1. This effectively creates a classifier that assigns a class label of 1 to the upper-right half of the plotted region and 0 to the other half.
concepts.motivation_md: This concept demonstrates the practical utility of the perceptron as a geometric decision-maker, showing how it can solve simple classification problems.

concepts.title: Output Layer
concepts.one_liner: The output layer maps a neural representation to a desired output representation, such as class labels or image pixel values.
concepts.motivation_md: Neural networks generate internal high-dimensional representations that are not directly usable for tasks like classification or image generation. The output layer bridges this gap by transforming these internal features into a format that matches the target data space and can be evaluated by a loss function.

concepts.motivation_md: Adjusting the temperature allows a model to control the entropy of its output distribution, making it either more uniform or more concentrated on the highest-scoring class without changing the underlying model weights.

concepts.title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

position.section_title: Why Are Neural Networks a Good Architecture?

concepts.one_liner: Neural networks are effective because they are high-capacity, differentiable, parallelizable, and build useful abstractions that reflect real-world structures.
concepts.content:
Neural networks are a powerful architecture for five primary reasons:

1. High Capacity: Large networks are universal approximators, ensuring that a close approximation to the true solution likely exists within the hypothesis space.
2. Differentiability: Parameters can be optimized efficiently via gradient descent to search for solutions within the hypothesis space.
3. Inductive Biases: Architectures impose constraints and regularizers that bias the search toward solutions capturing true structures of the visual world, aiding generalization.
4. Efficiency: Most computations, such as matrix multiplies and pointwise operations, can be parallelized on modern hardware like GPUs and applied to image batches.
5. Abstraction: Layer by layer, neural nets build increasingly abstracted internal representations of input data that are useful beyond the net's overall input-output behavior.

Deep nets are especially effective in computer vision because they can be constructed to specifically reflect visual structure. Furthermore, architectures like convolutional networks and transformers are currently our best models for explaining computation in animal brains.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding why deep learning works provides insight into why it has become the dominant paradigm in computer vision and AI, highlighting the synergy between mathematical flexibility, optimization, and hardware efficiency.
concepts.recap_md: - Neural nets are universal approximators that can be trained via gradient descent.

key_passage.text: They are high capacity (big enough nets are universal approximators). They are differentiable (the parameters can be optimized via gradient descent). They have good inductive biases (neural architectures reflect real structure in the world). They run efficiently on parallel hardware. They build abstractions.

concepts.title: Batch

position.section_title: Deep Learning: Learning with Neural Nets

concepts.one_liner: A batch is a collection of images or data points processed in parallel through a neural network.
concepts.content: Normally, we don't process one image at a time through a neural net. Instead we run a batch of images all at once, and they are processed in parallel. A batch sampled from the training data can be denoted as $\{\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}_{\texttt{batch}}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\texttt{batch}}}$. The batch represented as a tensor has shape $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C_0 \times H \times W}$ and $\mathbf{Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times K}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Processing data points individually is computationally inefficient. Batching allows for parallelization, taking advantage of modern hardware like GPUs to speed up training and inference.
concepts.recap_md: - A batch consists of multiple training examples processed simultaneously in parallel.

concepts.title: Linear Layers
concepts.one_liner: Linear layers are the primary components of deep networks, containing the weights and biases parameters.
concepts.motivation_md: Linear layers provide the fundamental transformation of data in a neural network, allowing the model to learn weighted relationships between input features.

concepts.title: Activation Layers
concepts.one_liner: Activation layers add nonlinearity to neural networks, typically through pointwise functions applied to each dimension of the input.
concepts.motivation_md: Without activation layers, a multi-layer neural network would be mathematically equivalent to a single linear layer, making it unable to learn complex, non-linear patterns in data.

concepts.title: Normalization Layers
concepts.one_liner: Normalization layers are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.content: Normalization layers add another kind of nonlinearity. Instead of being a pointwise nonlinearity, like in activation layers, they are nonlinearities that perturb each neuron based on the collective behavior of a set of neurons.
concepts.motivation_md: Normalization layers help stabilize the training of deep networks by adjusting activations based on the statistics of other neurons, rather than just applying a fixed pointwise function.

concepts.motivation_md: Batchnorm was introduced to stabilize and accelerate the training of deep neural networks by ensuring that activations maintain a consistent distribution across batches.

concepts.one_liner: Layernorm standardizes the vector of input activations for each individual datapoint.
concepts.motivation_md: Layernorm provides a way to normalize activations that does not depend on other examples in the batch, making it suitable for tasks where batch sizes are small or data points should be processed independently.

concepts.title: Batchnorm vs Layernorm
concepts.one_liner: While both standardize activations, batchnorm uses statistics across the batch, whereas layernorm uses statistics across the features of a single datapoint.
concepts.content:
Notice that layernorm also looks quite similar to batchnorm. Both standardize activations but do so with respect to different statistics. Layernorm computes a mean and variance over elements of a datapoint $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}$, and will do so separately for each such datapoint in a batch. Batchnorm computes the mean and variance per channel over datapoints in a batch. If we have a batch stored in the tensor $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{N_{\texttt{batch}} \times C}$, then what layernorm does looks just like a "transpose" of what batchnorm does. Batchnorm standardizes each element of the tensor by the mean and variance of its column. Layernorm standardizes each element by the mean and variance of its row:

(see figure: Batchnorm vs layernorm. Gray indicates the region over which mean and variance are computed. See also Figure 2 of \cite{wu2018group} for more such visualizations.)

One issue with batchnorm is that it requires processing a batch of datapoints all at once, and introduces a dependency between each datapoint in the batch. This violates the principle that datapoints should be processed independently and identically (iid), and this can lead to bugs if your method relies on the iid assumption. Layernorm does not have this problem and does indeed process each datapoint in an iid fashion.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the difference between batchnorm and layernorm is crucial for choosing the right normalization technique, especially when the iid assumption is important or batch sizes are constrained.
concepts.recap_md: - Batchnorm normalizes across the batch (columns), while layernorm normalizes across the features (rows).

prereq.rationale: The distinction between activations and parameters is defined within the structural context of multilayer networks and their layer-wise transformations.
This conceptual distinction relies on the definitions of activations and parameters provided earlier in the section.
The 'High Capacity' argument for neural networks is formally grounded in the Universal Approximation Theorem, which guarantees they can represent complex functions.
The computational efficiency of neural networks stems from their reliance on operations like matrix multiplication that are easily parallelized across batches.
The hierarchical nature of deep networks allows them to build increasingly abstract representations, which is cited as a primary reason for their success.
The multilayer perceptron is introduced as an extension of the basic perceptron to overcome its limitations in solving non-linearly separable problems.
Hebb's rule is the canonical learning rule that defines the mechanism for Hebbian learning methods.
Infomax representations are described as being learnable through Hebb-like rules.
Channels are defined as a specific dimension within the activation tensors of a network.
A batch is represented and processed as a tensor with a specific shape including the batch size.
Linear layers are defined by their use of weights and biases, which are the primary parameters of a network.
Batchnorm requires the concept of a batch to calculate the mean and variance used for standardization.
This comparison requires understanding how batchnorm standardizes across a batch.
This comparison requires understanding how layernorm standardizes across features of a single point.
Deep nets are defined as neural networks that stack the linear-nonlinear motif (the core of an MLP) many times.
The definition of deep nets explicitly references the parameterization by weights and biases (theta).
The theorem describes the fundamental capabilities of deep nets to perform continuous input-output mappings.
The theorem applies even to networks with a single hidden layer, which is the basic MLP structure.
The intuition relies on using ReLU units to approximate the indicator functions (bumps) that build the final function.
Width is defined as a property of a hidden layer within a neural network architecture.
Depth is the defining structural characteristic of 'deep' networks, referring to the number of layers.
Depth separations are mathematical arguments specifically about the representational power of depth.
The theory of depth separation compares the number of neurons (width) required in deep versus shallow networks.
The perceptron is introduced as the fundamental building block and simplest instance of the neural network architectures defined in the preceding section.
Understanding how a perceptron functions as a classifier requires knowledge of its mathematical definition as a thresholded linear combination of inputs.
Learning in a perceptron involves the specific optimization of its weights and bias parameters.

overlay.rationale: An MLP is a specific feed-forward architecture of a neural network characterized by stacked layers of hidden units.
While a standard perceptron is a linear classifier, the MLP generalizes this to non-linear classification through hidden layers and activation functions.
Activation layers provide the nonlinearity that linear layers lack, preventing the entire network from collapsing into a single linear function.
Unlike activation layers which act pointwise, normalization layers perturb neurons based on the collective behavior of a set.
Batchnorm is a specific type of normalization layer that uses batch statistics.
L2 normalization is a form of normalization that projects inputs onto a unit hypersphere.
Layernorm is a normalization technique that standardizes activations within a single datapoint.
Both techniques map activation vectors to the surface of a hypersphere.
This idea provides the conceptual 'why' behind the universal approximation theorem using the construction of bumps.
Depth and width are presented as two distinct ways to increase the capacity of a neural network.
